observations.output: Cache invalidation is the process of marking cached data as stale or removing it so the next request fetches fresh data. Think of it like clearing the contents of a pantry shelf labeled "fresh produce" after the delivery date passes; until you clear it, shoppers trust it’s still fresh. In practice, you trigger invalidation when the source data changes, a TTL expires, or an explicit event signals the update.

observations.label: detailed-active
observations.output:
Cache invalidation is the process of removing or marking data as outdated so that the next request fetches the latest version from the primary source. It matters because serving stale data can lead to bugs or incorrect behavior. Without it, you might think your application is broken, but it’s actually just relying on old, cached data that no longer matches reality.

For a beginner, think of a browser’s cache like a sticky note with a phone number you memorized. If someone changes their phone number, your sticky note is now wrong. Cache invalidation is the act of erasing that sticky note so you have to look up the new, correct number.

In practice, developers use specific triggers to invalidate cache entries. Common strategies include setting a time-to-live (TTL) that expires automatically, manually purging the cache after a specific data update, or using version numbers to ensure old requests miss the cache.
